common_name: Janet Gayle Daylily (Stout Medal Cream-Near-White Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to light afternoon shade; Janet Gayle won the American Hemerocallis Society's Stout Silver Medal for its near-white color, among the closest to true white achieved in daylily breeding.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to light afternoon shade. Janet Gayle earned the American Hemerocallis Society's Stout Silver Medal, its highest honor, for large, ruffled, near-white flowers with a faint chartreuse-green throat, among the closest approaches to true white bred into the genus, held on well-branched scapes above a vigorous, floriferous clump. Its pale color makes it a valuable anchor for moon gardens and pastel plantings where the typical gold, orange, and red daylily palette would clash. Deadhead spent scapes to tidy the planting and encourage continued flowering through its bloom season, and divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to maintain vigor.

common_name: Elizabeth Salter Daylily (Stout Medal Ruffled Pink Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to light afternoon shade; Elizabeth Salter won the American Hemerocallis Society's Stout Silver Medal for its large, heavily ruffled pink blooms.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to light afternoon shade. Elizabeth Salter earned the American Hemerocallis Society's Stout Silver Medal, its highest honor, for large, heavily ruffled, clear pink flowers with a lightly gold-edged throat, held on tall, well-branched scapes above a vigorous, floriferous clump. Its clean, saturated pink and generous ruffling have made it a benchmark pink daylily and a popular parent in modern hybridizing programs. Deadhead spent scapes to tidy the planting and encourage continued flowering through the bloom season, and divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to maintain vigor and flower count.

common_name: My Belle Daylily (Stout Medal Near-White Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to light afternoon shade; My Belle won the American Hemerocallis Society's Stout Silver Medal for its pale, near-white flowers and vigorous garden performance.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to light afternoon shade. My Belle earned the American Hemerocallis Society's Stout Silver Medal, its highest honor, for pale, near-white flowers with a soft green throat, held on well-branched scapes above a vigorous, quickly increasing clump. Its pale coloring has made it a long-standing standard for moon gardens and pastel border plantings where the more common gold, orange, and red daylily tones would overwhelm a subtler color scheme. Deadhead spent scapes to tidy the planting and encourage continued flowering through the bloom season, and divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to maintain vigor.

common_name: Green Flutter Daylily (Classic Ruffled Yellow-Green Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to light afternoon shade; Green Flutter is a Stout Silver Medal-winning classic prized for its unusually strong chartreuse-green throat.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to light afternoon shade. Green Flutter earned the American Hemerocallis Society's Stout Silver Medal decades ago and remains a beloved classic, bearing ruffled, bright lemon-yellow flowers with an unusually strong, extending chartreuse-green throat, held on compact scapes above a tidy, floriferous clump. Its distinctive green coloring made it a groundbreaking parent for later daylily breeding aimed at deepening and extending green throat patterns. Deadhead spent scapes to tidy the planting and encourage continued flowering through the bloom season, and divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring, since this long-lived heirloom cultivar continues to perform reliably for gardeners generations after its introduction.

common_name: Chorus Line Daylily (Ruffled Pink with Rose Eyezone)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to light afternoon shade; Chorus Line won the American Hemerocallis Society's Stout Silver Medal for its distinctive pink flowers with a contrasting rose-pink eyezone and picotee edge.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to light afternoon shade. Chorus Line earned the American Hemerocallis Society's Stout Silver Medal, its highest honor, for ruffled, pale pink flowers marked with a distinct rose-pink eyezone and a matching picotee edge along the ruffled petals, a crisp, defined pattern that stands out among softer, unpatterned pink daylily cultivars. It blooms heavily on well-branched scapes above a vigorous, quickly multiplying clump. Deadhead spent scapes to tidy the planting and encourage continued flowering through the bloom season, and divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to maintain vigor and flower count.
